To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
opaque selling is a better strategy than direct last-minute sales for a company that sells a perishable product to consumers with rational expectations.

opaque selling is preferred over direct lastminute selling when consumer valuations are low or service differentiation is large, or both; that opaque selling is more preferred over direct sales as the probability of a high-demand period increases; and that the efficacy of opaque sales is reduced when service providers have different capacities.
opaque selling is preferred over direct lastminute selling when the probability of high consumer demand is low and when the probability of having a high consumer valuation for the service is high.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the strategic use of last-minute sales and opaque selling by service providers.
the strategic implications of using last-minute sales to sell excess capacity.
the strategic use of opaque selling by service providers to manage customer behavior, as well as to manage their own capacity and revenue risks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
opaque selling is a more efficient way of dealing with the last-minute demand than direct last-minute selling.
opaque selling is preferred when the service is homogeneous or when there are many competing providers, whereas direct last-minute sales dominate in the opposite cases.
opaque selling should be used when there is low service differentiation and high consumer valuations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the opaque selling strategy can be used to increase revenues when the probability of high-demand periods is high, when service differentiation between competing providers is low, or when consumer valuations are high.
opaque selling is more effective when consumers have low valuations for travel or when there are significant differences among competing service providers.
opaque selling is more likely to be used when the service provider has a high level of capacity, and the service has a high degree of substitutability among competing service providers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
last-minute sales and opaque selling are not mutually exclusive strategies, but rather they are substitutes.
opaque selling is not just a mechanism to dispose of unused capacity but can be a strategic tool to influence consumer purchasing behavior.
the use of opaque selling is not necessarily a mechanism for disposing unused capacity, but can be an effective mechanism to manage demand in a strategic manner.
